title: The crypto revolving door: officials who moved to firms they shaped policy for
summary: Most of the named moves are documented. Bo Hines left the White House crypto council on 9 Aug 2025, joined Tether on 19 Aug and became CEO of its US arm (USAT) on 12 Sep 2025. Per the WSJ (14 Oct 2026), a firm he co-owned, Nxum, had a $415K-a-month Tether deal from May 2025 and received about $6.3M, and Sen. Blumenthal opened an inquiry on 22 Oct 2026. Caroline Pham (CFTC to MoonPay), Summer Mersinger (CFTC to Blockchain Association) and Brian Quintenz (a16z/Kalshi to a withdrawn CFTC nomination to SUI Group's board) are also documented. So are the industry ties Mike Selig, Paul Atkins and Jonathan Gould brought into office, and Steve Witkoff's retained World Liberty holdings as special envoy. Gaps: I found no waiver or cooling-off record for Hines or Gould, no named 2025-26 SEC staff move to Coinbase or a16z, and no finding by any authority that a move broke ethics rules.

sub_claims.statement: Bo Hines went from director of the White House crypto council to running Tether's US arm (USAT).
sub_claims.finding: Hines was executive director of the President's Council of Advisers on Digital Assets from Jan 2025 and announced his departure on 9 Aug 2025. Tether named him strategic adviser for digital assets and US strategy on 19 Aug 2025, ten days later. On 12 Sep 2025 Tether unveiled USAT and named him CEO of the US business, based in Charlotte. Anchorage Digital Bank is the issuer and Cantor Fitzgerald the reserve custodian (see C35). USAT launched on 27 Jan 2026. Some early reports called him 'CEO of Tether USA' as early as August; Bloomberg and others called him an adviser until the September announcement.

sub_claims.statement: Hines's move raises cooling-off/ethics issues (payments from Tether while he shaped stablecoin policy).
sub_claims.finding: The WSJ reported on 14 Oct 2026 (known here through secondary coverage) that Tether agreed in May 2025 to pay Nxum, a consulting firm Hines co-founded and still owned a third of while in government, $415,000 a month for lobbying, PR and advisory work. About $6.3M reportedly flowed. Early payments were routed through a marketing firm, Notorious, and later ones, including two of $2.49M in Dec 2025 and Apr 2026, went straight to Nxum after Hines left. The WSJ also reported that Hines pushed for the GENIUS Act's three-year transition period, a provision favourable to Tether. On 22 Oct 2026 Sen. Blumenthal (PSI ranking member) wrote to Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino and to Nxum CEO Todd Hines, Bo's father, asking for contracts and payment records by 3 Nov 2026 (one outlet says 6 Nov). His letter says the arrangement implicates ethics, anticorruption and lobbying laws, and that Nxum never registered its lobbying. No public ethics waiver or post-employment determination for Hines was found. No authority has found a violation, and the reporting does not show the money changed any provision.

sub_claims.statement: Brian Quintenz (Kalshi board) had his CFTC chair nomination withdrawn.
sub_claims.finding: Quintenz was a CFTC commissioner in Trump's first term, then a16z crypto's global head of policy and a Kalshi board member (reportedly since 2021). He pledged to leave the Kalshi board if confirmed, and his Kalshi ties drew gaming-industry opposition. Trump nominated him in early 2025. After months of delay and a public feud with the Winklevoss twins, who urged Trump to drop him (Quintenz released their texts), the White House withdrew the nomination on 30 Sep 2025; it was reported on 1 Oct. Mike Selig was nominated instead. Quintenz joined SUI Group's board (Nasdaq: SUIG) as an independent director effective 5 Jan 2026. He was also reported as a senior adviser to a prediction-markets coalition backing Kalshi, but I could not confirm the date. Note: as a withdrawn nominee he never held office in this administration, so this is an industry-to-nominee-to-industry path, not a classic revolving-door exit.

Before government, Selig was a Willkie Farr & Gallagher partner. He represented crypto clients including eToro and Paradigm, and The Intercept's review of his ethics records (26 Nov 2025) adds venture firms, a Cayman Islands blockchain company, Architect Financial Technologies and trade groups such as the Blockchain Association. He was chief counsel of the SEC's Crypto Task Force in 2025, was confirmed CFTC chair on 18 Dec 2025 (53-43, see C25) and was sworn in on 22 Dec 2025. Per The Intercept, his ethics agreement makes him step back from former clients' matters only for the standard one year after his last service, with no broader recusal. The full client list rests on The Intercept and his OGE filing; I could not read either directly.

sub_claims.statement: Paul Atkins's prior crypto clients and holdings.
sub_claims.finding: Atkins founded Patomak Global Partners, whose clients reportedly included banks, crypto exchanges and DeFi platforms. FTX signed on in early 2022. His OGE disclosure, made public on 25 Mar 2025, showed up to ~$327M in family assets and up to ~$6M in crypto-related assets: about $1M of Anchorage Digital equity, Securitize call options worth $2.5-5M, and a small Pontoro stake. He reported no direct crypto. He pledged to resign from Patomak and divest within 90 days of confirmation, and to stay out of matters involving Patomak or its clients for one year. On 6 Aug 2025 Sen. Warren asked him to name the buyer and the price; the SEC said he complies with his ethics agreement, and no buyer has been disclosed in what I found. Barron's (Aug 2025) reported that defendants in a Trump Media lawsuit sought Patomak records on any TMTG engagement. TMTG called this 'meritless' and denied engaging Patomak.

sub_claims.statement: Jonathan Gould (OCC) came from crypto firm Bitfury.
sub_claims.finding: Gould was senior deputy comptroller and chief counsel at the OCC (2018-21), then Bitfury's chief legal officer from 2022 (Law.com). He was earlier a Jones Day partner. He was confirmed Comptroller 50-45 on 10 Jul 2025, and his OCC granted World Liberty's trust-bank charter preliminary conditional approval on 14 Aug 2026 (see C12). I found no public ethics agreement, recusal list or waiver covering Bitfury or crypto-charter matters. Reports of Warren seeking a four-year recusal come only from a low-reliability dossier site and are unverified.

sub_claims.statement: David Sacks (AI & crypto czar) kept industry holdings under ethics waivers.
sub_claims.finding: Established in C34. He served as a special government employee under ethics waivers (crypto, 5 Mar 2025; AI, mid-2025) while Craft Ventures kept AI-linked stakes and a 7.8% BitGo stake. He stepped down as czar around 26-27 Mar 2026 and became PCAST co-chair. Sacks denies any conflict.

sub_claims.statement: SEC/CFTC officials departed to crypto firms (Coinbase, a16z, etc.).
sub_claims.finding: The clearest cases are at the CFTC. Acting Chair Caroline Pham's move to MoonPay as chief legal and administrative officer was announced on 17 Dec 2025, to start when her CFTC service ended; MoonPay said she would lead its Washington policy strategy. Commissioner Summer Mersinger's move to Blockchain Association CEO was announced on 14 May 2025; she started on 2 Jun 2025, leaving a term that ran to Apr 2028, and was reported in Sep 2026 to be stepping down at year-end. Former SEC Trading & Markets director Brett Redfearn, a first-term official, went to Coinbase and then became Securitize's president in Apr 2026. Securitize was an Atkins holding. Traffic also runs the other way: Selig moved from industry law to the SEC to the CFTC, and Taylor Lindman, Chainlink's deputy GC, became SEC Crypto Task Force chief counsel on 23 Feb 2026. I could not name any 2025-26 SEC staffer who moved to Coinbase or a16z specifically; one Jan 2026 headline about a Coinbase hire was too thin to rely on. The widely cited count of 200+ officials (28 SEC, 15 CFTC) comes from a Tech Transparency Project study cited in Oct 2022 congressional letters, so it predates this administration.

sub_claims.statement: Hines's successor Patrick Witt also left for industry.
sub_claims.finding: Witt was Hines's deputy and took the executive director post in Aug 2025. He had been a Pentagon technology official and acting director of the Office of Strategic Capital. He announced his exit on 14 Oct 2026 as the CLARITY Act stalled and said he would go to the private sector. No employer had been reported in what I found.

sub_claims.statement: Trump family business partners were placed in government roles.
sub_claims.finding: Steve Witkoff co-founded World Liberty Financial with the Trump sons; his son Zach is WLF's CEO. He became Special Envoy. WLF said in May 2025 that he was divesting, yet his 13 Aug 2025 disclosure still listed WLF crypto holdings and WC Digital Fi LLC shares. Senators led by Schiff and Warren queried OGE (Oct 2025), and Warren and Murphy opened an inquiry on 18 Nov 2025. A spokesperson said he does not take part in matters affecting his financial interests. Howard Lutnick's Cantor-Tether ties (C35) are a second example. I did not find a systematic list of family business partners in government posts.

corrections: The brief calls Quintenz part of an official-to-industry move, but he never took office in this administration. His nomination was withdrawn on 30 Sep 2025, and his Kalshi board seat predated the nomination.
Hines was first a Tether 'strategic adviser' (19 Aug 2025). He became CEO of the US arm/USAT on 12 Sep 2025, not on leaving the White House.
The '200+ officials' revolving-door count (Tech Transparency Project) dates from 2022 and does not measure this administration.
No 2025-26 SEC staff move to Coinbase or a16z was confirmed. The best-documented departures are CFTC leaders (Pham to MoonPay, Mersinger to Blockchain Association).
denials_and_context: Nxum's representative said Hines did not know of the Tether deal and received no Tether funds while at the White House. Tether says an external-counsel investigation found no wrongdoing.
The SEC says Atkins complies with his ethics agreement, and Trump Media called the Patomak subpoena inquiry 'meritless'.
Witkoff's spokesperson says he does not take part in matters that could affect his financial interests. WLF says neither Trump nor Witkoff was involved in the UAE-linked $2B MGX deal.
Selig's and Atkins's one-year recusals are the standard federal ethics pledge, not special treatment. Critics argue it is too short for officials writing rules for the whole industry.
Industry-to-regulator hiring (Lindman, Selig) is defended as bringing technical expertise. Revolving-door hiring in crypto also predates this administration, as the TTP 2022 study shows.
Searches did not show any of these moves violating 18 U.S.C. 207 or a signed ethics pledge. The concerns rest on timing, payments and congressional letters.
